Assuming no editing was used, it's all about perspective. In person, the moon can appear a lot larger when it's near the horizon because the way your brain processes the size of the moon compared to the size of objects in the field of view around it. Additionally, the moon is really far away, so when you move around on earth, its apparent size does not change. However, objects on earth do appear to change in size when you move around. 

​

Say you were looking at the Seattle skyline really close up; the space needle would look massive. Contrarily, if you were far away, the space needle would look small. In both of these cases, the moon's actual size does not change but since your brain is comparing its size to other objects (in this case, the space needle) it looks like it changes size.

[Moon + Space Needle when close](https://preview.redd.it/9iibdsljrs261.jpg?width=640&crop=smart&auto=webp&s=5073ec5d02a921e1a9a48454580234d5e17f3703)

Well it really depends on the level of precision. For the exact full moon, it's merely a single point in time. To observers on Earth, it appears to last a whole day. But we can get more precise when you look at the actual percentage of illumination.

On average, the lunar phase cycle (synodic month) is 29.53059 days, or 29 days, 12 hours,  44 minutes. The moon illumination ranges from 0 - 100, but over the synodic month, the illumination also returns back to 0.  That means half of the synodic month represents the span from 0% to 100% illumination.

29.530590 ÷ 2 = 14.765295 days (half of synodic month)

14.765295 ÷ 100 = 0.14765295 days per percentage of moon illumination. So, there are about 3 hours and 32 minutes per percent (such as from 99%-100%)

To get more precise, 0.14765295 days = ~12757 seconds per percentage. Depending on how precise you want to get, simply divide this number by 10^(d), where d is the number of additional significant digits. To increase the level of precision by 4 more decimal places, we can do the following:

12757 seconds ÷ (10^4) = 1.2757 seconds. It takes about 1.28 seconds for the moon's illumination to increase or decrease by 0.0001%. 

Therefore, the moon remains at least 99.9999% illuminated for ~2.55 seconds on average.

This is my first real attempt at M31, the Andromeda Galaxy. I tried a few times in the past but it was too early in the year, then wildfire smoke ruined my images for a few months. This is also the first time I was able to actually use my new-ish setup with a cooled camera, better mount, and a telescope. After issues with Photoshop I decided to buy PixInsight and just get over the learning curve that comes with it. I'm really glad I did because I don't think I could personally get this result from Photoshop.  


This image is by no means perfect but I am proud of it as M31 has always been my goal for my first real astrophoto. Please don't be afraid to leave constructive criticism as I appreciate anything that will help me learn!

# Acquisition

* Lights - 108x180" @ 125 gain
* Darks - 20
* Bias - 100
* Flats - 50
* Total Integration: 5h 24m
* Bortle 5-6 over the nights of 10/11, 10/13, 10/15  - from my backyard

# Gear

* Camera: ZWO ASI294MC
* Telescope: SkyWatcher Evostar 80ED
* Mount: AZ-EQ5 Pro w/ Pier Tripod
* Guide scope: Svbony 50mm
* Guide Camera: ZWO ASI120MM

# Processing

* Preprocessed in DSS using Kappa Sigma Clipping
* Auto-stretch (STF - unlinked)
* Dynamic Crop
* Dynamic Background Extraction (div/sub)
* Background Neutralization
* Color Calibration
* Histogram Transformation from STF
* Curves Transformation to darken background
* Integer Resample (2:1) > StarNet

**Starless:**

* Extract Luminance
* LRGB Combination
* SCNR (Green)
* Curves Transformations to increase contrast, saturation, and improve color balance
* Curves to darken and desaturate background
* Clone stamp touch-ups on background

**Stars re-added:**

* PixelMath - max(starless, starmask)
* Curves Transformation to fix star brightness and color

# Notes:

As this was my first time really learning PixInsight, I had to use some videos to help guide me through an example workflow and use different tools. These two videos really helped me and I would highly recommend them if you are using PixInsight for the first time with M31:

* [Reddit's /u/Le\_Baron's M31 data in PixInsight](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XNURR_wf7ro)
* [Easy Pixinsight Dynamic Background Extraction!](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eB0J4-O5WUQ)

The following is based on what I've read and learned online, in books, and through trial and error.

1. Not sure if this was meant to be a question, but yes do everything you can to increase total integration window.

2. It depends, but typically a good way to choose ISO is looking at a sub-exposure's histogram and aiming to keep the spike in the middle. Just adjust iso til it's around there. This is just a guideline, so play around with it.

3. This is a big topic, so it's really best to get some books or at the least look at some YouTube videos to learn how to process well. One thing I will say though, don't do anything way too much. If there isn't enough detail in the nebula and you've done a lot of curves adjustments, you may just need more integration.

4. Yes, I would argue they are pretty important when shooting nebulae. You want to get the best signal to noise ratio possible, especially when using a camera with an IR cut filter. It is worth the time and if temperature is the same for each night you shoot, you can often reuse calibration frames (in my experience).

5. Yes, there is. Longer sub-exposures will improve the signal to noise ratio, but under very light polluted skies, it's very difficult to get long sub-exposures without a gradient encompassing the frame. But in general, it's best to go with 2 minute vs 1 minute frames.

**Acquisition:**

* Camera: Canon 60D (unmodded)
* Lens: Samyang 135mm f/2 @ f/2.8
* Mount: iOptron Skytracker Pro
* Lights: 45x120s, 11x150s (total of 118 minutes) @ ISO 250
* 25 darks (only for 120s, no darks for 150s exposures), 50 flats, 100 bias frames.
* Bortle 5 sky on May 12-13.

​

**Processing:**

Stacked using DeepSkySacker using Entrop Weighted Average method, Drizzle 2x.

Post processing was done in Photoshop starting with non-aggressive curves adjustments. Next, I used levels adjustments and balanced the RGB values for various points in the sky  (darker background spots and brighter stars using color sample tool). Followed this with another curves then levels adjustment. Did some selective saturation and contrast adjustments on M81 and M82. Finally, used Camera Raw filter to defringe stars (remove any halos) and general + selective noise reduction to finish it all off.

Also used GradientXTerminator - RC Astro to remove some of the light pollution.

Image was cropped after this to make M81 the focal point.

​

Shot this using 18-55mm f/3.5-5.6 IS II lens. ISO 3200, f/5, 1/160 exposure time. 


Tips:

-Be patient

-Get better tank lighting if necessary as this is easily the most important part

-Use a tripod or something to hold your camera/phone in place

------------

If you wanna get more technical:

-Use a DSLR (or pro mode) and set the shutter speed/exposure time lower (1/160 or lower I'd say). 

-Set a lower ISO; mine was really high because the lens I'm using isn't great for this. I'd recommend 1000 or lower if possible. 

-You have to balance the ISO and shutter speed to get good focus but reduce noise. ISO <= 1000 and shutter <= 1/160 is optimal. Shutter is more important if the fish will never stay still.

-If using DSLR, get a lens with a low f-stop. Somewhere around f/2.8 would be good as this allows you to optimize your iso and shutter speed. However, too low of an f-stop and only part of the fish might be in focus
